title: How subjective should a film video essay be?

commenti.body: I like subjective ones the most. Tell me what you think about the movie.  Many just rehash the same old things or something they read.  Give me your view and maybe I will see and learn something new.  Talk about things you like: the look of the movie, a particular actor, a certain scene, the music or something else. It can be controversial or against popular opinion but then say why.

Any film essay will be subjective, and I’d be more worried about ones that impose objectivity or pose that they obviously know what the director intended. I think the best video essay within that has room for plenty of subjectivity while still referencing an “objective” model of what most people might say about a specific film. Even if the point is to disagree with that model, I think a good basis is professionalism and goods-faith takes.

I rarely watch (because rarely like) video essays, specially anglophone ones, because they always try to explain:

- The director's intentions (while you can't guess them, and that they're pretty much irrelevant in analysis anyway)

- Finding some "objective rules" on why it works (as is there was one way to do things well for each kind of scene), reducing all an art to a question of functionality (and doing like if the meaning of the scene went "without saying", like if it was not even a matter of interpretation or ambiguity).

- Explaining why the film is so good or so bad (while it's just not the point when you studying something, and subjective anyway)

The few video I liked the most is when people talk about what they really care. What interest them specially, even if it's a detail.

- You like to guess the repercussion of all the crew member of the team on that film, because you follow their career and know that the guy who made those costums in that blockbuster the year before wanted to work with this other one, or wathever? Cool, give me that, drowned me in a geek knowledge I know nothing of about how a production works.

- You like to do a total and subjective exegesis on how every movie deep down tell the story of the bible? Or how which scene remind you the feeling of this one you saw as a kid in another films, and why? Cool, give me your visions.

- You like to explore each scene on how they use color because it's your passion, and ONLY that? Cool, open that door on the way you look at films for me.

- You're a bookworm and you have no personal idea, but like to do a mash-up of all the research, critics, theories that exist on a specific scene? Cool, you will give me a general idea of the theories on it.

Do YOUR ting, and don't try to be teacher, like a top of the class doing his homework well, and a complete dissection. Good and stimulating insights on movies never and will never look like that.

I think the primary point of enjoyment is that it be well thought out, subjective or not. A video essay that makes an interesting analysis of the techniques used, or the content of the story, is far better than some nasal voiced white teen reading a synopsis and just giving a shallow opinion, AKA 90% of video essays. 

I don’t think there’s a hard and fast rule. I like many dash are subjective, I like many that are not. But I only like them if they’re substantive and go deeper than just regurgitating a plot synopsis. Subjectivity is probably more interesting because the essayist has to stand behind their claims and give examples of what they’re analyzing, but simply presenting techniques is good too
Agree with this. I enjoy hearing people talk about what they're passionate about, even if I have no relationship to it, as long as they aren't trying to speak for anyone else.

First of all the technical details, the facts behind the making of the movie, the info and facts about directors, actors, writers, etc, details about filmic language, acting, etc. Comparison and similarities to other movies. 

Then, explanations of metaphors, symbols, plot, meanings, etc. Going deep into expressive art of movies, making also comparisons to other forms of art ( paintings, literature, music, etc) 

In the end subjective opinions, but justified, explained. 

What matters more is expertise, knowledge, competence, depth of mind, language skills of the reviewer. 

And above all, honesty, sincerity, independence. No endorsement, no promotion of movies as hidden and not declared business. It's better to have sponsors not related to movies to make some honest money.
